chunks: My father (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Sabah ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, Hisham, Hafs, and others. They said:
Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) said: We believe neither in fatalism nor in delegation.

key_terms.تَفْوِيض: Tafwid (delegation): the belief that God has fully delegated control to humans, removing divine involvement from human affairs. Attributed to some Mu'tazili scholars.
key_terms.جَبْر: Jabr (fatalism/compulsion): the belief that all human actions are predetermined by God, leaving no room for free will. Attributed to the Jabriyyah school.

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about fatalism (jabr) and delegation (tafwid) regarding free will?
ai.summary: This hadith transmits Imam al-Sadiq's concise articulation of the Shia doctrine of 'al-amr bayn al-amrayn' (the matter between the two matters) regarding divine decree and human free will. By rejecting both 'jabr' (compulsion/fatalism, the belief that humans have no free will) and 'tafwid' (delegation, the belief that God has delegated complete autonomy to humans), the Imam establishes the middle position that humans have a measure of free will within the framework of divine sovereignty. This principle became a cornerstone of Shia theology, distinguishing it from both the Jabri and Mu'tazili positions.
